title: Friends of other faiths
hook: friendship across faiths, each keeping their own
tomorrow: a fight against Moses. why does the Mishnah leave Moses out?

segments.voice: Yesterday, every person in the image of God, so you stand up for anyone targeted. Every image. Today, the friend across the line, up close.

Pizza boxes on the stage after closing night. Owen came, who grew up Lutheran, and Yasmin from the crew, who is Muslim. What does each keep? Their own. And late in the night, the questions get real. Owen asks: so what do you actually think happens to me? It's easier to change the subject. The Talmud keeps a friendship built on questions like that, between Rabbi Judah the Prince and a Roman it calls Antoninus. One day Antoninus brings a hard one. After death, he says, body and soul can both get off. The body says: the soul did it. The soul says: the body did it. So who gets judged?
screen: `PIZZA ON THE STAGE.` → `EACH KEEPS THEIR OWN.` → `A RABBI AND A ROMAN.` → `BODY AND SOUL: NOT ME.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Judah answers the way friends do: with a story. A king has an orchard of fine early figs, and he sets two guards, one who can't walk and one who can't see. The one who can't walk says: I see beautiful figs. Carry me. So he rides on the shoulders of the one who can't see, and together they eat the figs. The king comes back. The first says: me? I have no legs. The second says: me? I have no eyes. So the king sets one on the other's shoulders and judges them together. Body and soul, the rabbi says, answer as one. Now notice what the scene doesn't do. Nobody asks the other to switch. The question is real, the answer is real, and the Talmud tells other talks between the two of them as well. Another page of the Talmud puts this kind of friendship to work: support the poor of other peoples along with your own, visit their sick, bury their dead, because of darkhei shalom, the ways of peace. In that picture, friendship across faiths isn't pretending you agree. It's honesty about where you stand, and showing up anyway. Something to tell a friend tonight: the Talmud's answer to a Roman's hardest question is a story about two guards stealing figs.
screen: `TWO GUARDS IN AN ORCHARD.` · `JUDGED TOGETHER.` · `NOBODY ASKS THE OTHER TO SWITCH.` · `THE WAYS OF PEACE.` · then, large: `FRIENDS ACROSS FAITHS.`

segments.voice: Open a message to a friend whose faith, or lack of one, isn't yours. Write one honest question you've never asked them, about something they keep and why it matters to them. Read it once, then send it, or save it for when you're face to face.
screen: `ONE FRIEND, ANOTHER FAITH.` · `ONE HONEST QUESTION.` · `SEND IT, OR SAVE IT.`

segments.voice: Friends of other faiths: a friendship across a line of belief, where each keeps their own and the questions stay honest.
Keep this: friends across faiths. Two guards, one orchard, each carrying the other a little. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jewish tradition keeps stories of friendship across faiths, like Rabbi Judah the Prince and the Roman Antoninus trading questions, and the Talmud teaches caring for the poor, the sick and the dead of other peoples because of the ways of peace.

chat.meaning: Rabbi Judah and Antoninus asked each other real questions. Friendship across faiths is honesty, each keeping their own, not pretending it's all the same.
